extracted.intended_audience: poets, writers, literary critics, and informed readers of poetry/ballads
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging heroic poems and popular ballads, emphasizing simplicity, naturalness, moral precept, national subjects, and accessibility to common readers. Includes how to test reception and what kinds of incidents, diction, and character behavior to employ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of Appeal / Human Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Human Nature is the same in all reasonable Creatures; and whatever falls in with it, will meet with Admirers amongst Readers of all Qualities and Conditions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose elements that accord with common human sensibilities; a work that 'falls in with' human nature will please readers across classes. Examples: songs and simple paintings of nature delight both ordinary and refined readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of Thought and Style
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the essential and inherent Perfection of Simplicity of Thought' — simplicity pleases all kinds of palates, unlike a 'Gothick Manner' or artificial taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor straightforward, natural expression over affected or epigrammatic flourishes. Illustration: Homer, Virgil, Milton (when language is understood) please plain readers; epigrammatists like Martial or Cowley do not. Anti-pattern: over-stylized 'Gothick' manner that only gratifies a small, artificial audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test Reception with Ordinary Readers
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece's likely success can be judged by its reception among simple, everyday people (Molière read to his housekeeper and children to predict audience laughter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before publication/performance, try passages on unpretentious listeners (housekeeper, children, common folk); their spontaneous responses predict broader public reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational Moral Precept Adapted to Country
rubrics_metrics.description: 'an Heroick Poem should be founded upon some important Precept of Morality, adapted to the Constitution of the Country in which the Poet writes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the poem around a moral or civic lesson that resonates with the poet's society and political constitution. Examples: Homer grounding union among Greeks; Virgil addressing Roman ideals. Anti-pattern: heroic subjects divorced from local moral/political relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate Persons and Actions that Honour the Country
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic poems should 'celebrate Persons and Actions which do Honour to their Country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects—heroes, deeds—that reflect national virtue and raise the nation's reputation. Avoid celebrating foreign or irrelevant exploits (example: critique of Valerius Flaccus and Statius for choosing the Golden Fleece/Wars of Thebes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer National/Local Heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer to 'find out an Hero in his own Country' to enhance the poem's effect and patriotic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a hero from the poet's own nation increases the audience's emotional investment and the poem's reputational benefit for the country (illustrated by the English hero in Chevy-Chase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Beautiful, Reputation-Raising Incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Include 'beautiful Incidents' that raise the reputation of the country and the hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose scenes that showcase valor, honor, and national character through vivid incidents (e.g., contrasts between English and Scottish conduct in the quoted ballad). Such incidents should serve both aesthetic and patriotic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw an Instructional Moral from the Poem
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem should conclude (or include) a Precept for the Benefit of its Readers (the poet draws a precept from the narrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the instructive purpose explicit enough to guide readers toward the intended moral (example: final four lines of the ballad urging an end to noble quarrels). Anti-pattern: narrative without discernible moral aim in heroic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and 'Majestick Simplicity' over Epigrammatical Wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The ballad's 'sentiments... are extremely natural and poetical, and full of the majestick Simplicity which we admire in the greatest of the ancient Poets'—avoid epigrammatic turns and points of wit in such pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For songs and ballads aimed at wide emotional effect, prioritize natural sentiment and simple majesty rather than clever conceits. Anti-pattern: over-clever epigrams that spoil the popular appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of Language to Reach Plain Readers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'so far as the Language of their Poems is understood, will please a Reader of plain common Sense'—language must be comprehensible to common readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diction and syntax accessible to the intended audience; opaque or overly learned language limits comprehension and appeal. Example contrast: Homer/Virgil/Milton (when understood) vs Martial/Cowley.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Diction and 'Apparel' for the Subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The external 'Apparel' (diction/style) must suit the subject; rustic or ancient songs should not be needlessly embellished, though some passages may be 'gorgeous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match register to content: plain subjects call for plain apparel; poetry may occasionally be elevated, but do so in harmony with the poem's genius. Anti-pattern: dressing a rude song in artificial high style that undermines its natural force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic Sentiments and Actions Must Suit the Hero
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' sentiments and actions should be 'every Way suitable to an Hero'—behaviour and speech must align with heroic status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft dialogue and deeds that display magnanimity, courage, and nobility appropriate to heroic figures (examples: single combat proposals, magnanimous lamentations, exhortations to continue the battle after death). Avoid incongruous behavior that diminishes heroic stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ Vivid, Natural Detail to Move Readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete, natural particulars (taking the dead by the hand, riding a milk-white steed, armour shining like gold) to evoke feeling and grandeur akin to the ancients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select striking, tactile images and simple dramatic actions that produce emotional resonance; parallel examples to lines from the Æneid and other classics to achieve majesty without artificiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity Should Not Be Read as Lack of Grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: 'not to let the Simplicity of the Stile... prejudice him against the Greatness of the Thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and readers should recognise that humble diction can carry profound and majestic ideas; writers should trust simple expression when the thought is great.
